<h4> I DIDN'T UNDERSTAND THE POIS FUNCTIONS SO HERE IS A HINT I CREATED FOR MYSELF: 

* dpois(k,λ,log) where, 
* K: number of successful events happened in an interval 
* lambda: mean per interval 
* log: If TRUE then the function returns probability in form of log 


## What is the probability that she will hear more than 8 calls during any given session?
```{r}
#ppois() calculates the probability of a random variable that will be equal to or less than a number
#I am very bad at statistics and don't entirely understand the goal of this function (I am interpreting it as the probability that the number of calls will be greater than the K value I assign - here I start with 8)
lambda <- 15
y <- ppois(8, lambda, lower.tail = FALSE) # I think I am saying FALSE here because that prevents my probability from being read as a log (but unsure totally)
y
```
## What is the probability that she will hear no calls in a session?
```{r}
lambda <- 15
# I am not sure if I should make custom value labels (i.e. "no calls") or just use X or a different variable (here I did y)?
y <- dpois(0, lambda, FALSE) #dpois is used to determine the probability that that event will occur based on the mean? (Probability Density Function)
y
```
## What is the probability that she will hear exactly 3 calls in a session?
```{r}
lambda <- 15
y <- dpois(3, lambda, FALSE) #Again I am using #dpois to determine the probability that a specific number of events will occur
y
```

## Plot the relevant Poisson mass function over the values in range 0 ≤ x ≤ 30.  
```{r}
x <- 0:30 
lambda <- 15 # go back and do this for all chunks if you are going to assign it here again
y <- dpois(x, lambda) #this assigns the y axis as all of the predicted probabilities that correspond to the x values 1:30

plot(x, y, type = "histogram", lwd = 3, main = "Poisson Mass Function (λ = 15)",
     xlab = "Number of Calls", ylab = "Probability")
#For "type =" can I just put h instead of histogram? does it make a difference if i do it the other way?
#lwd changes the line width
#main sets the title and x and y lab sets the axes labels
points(x, y, pch = 15, col = "pink") #different options for pch when making this plot (16 sets it to a filled in circle)

```

## Simulate 104 results from this distribution (i.e., 2 years of Saturday monitoring sessions).Plot the simulated results using hist() and use xlim() to set the horizontal limits to be from 0 to 30. How does your histogram compare to the shape of the probability mass function you plotted above?
#### (I combined these two parts because I felt like it made more sense being able to generate random data in one part and then make a histogram in another)
```{r}
#here is where i am generating random data with the n = 104, set.seed lets me reproduce my data when i run it again (i'm not sure about the 1234 i saw some variation between that and 123 in the textbook) 
set.seed(12345) 
lambda <- 15
r <- rpois(n = 104, lambda = 15)

#now making my histogram
hist(r, freq = FALSE, col.lab = "#e01485", col.main = "#e01485", 
     col = "#f0a5ea",
     border = "#e01485",  # sets border color to pink
     main = "Simulated Data (n=104) and Their Associated Probabilities",
     xlab = "Number of Calls (X)", xlim = c(0, 30),
     ylab = "Probability",
     axes = FALSE) #okay this removes the default black x and y axis lines with the tick marks
axis(1, col = "#e01485", col.axis = "#e01485")  # X-axis
axis(2, col = "#e01485", col.axis = "#e01485")  # Y-axis, i set color of axis here individually instead of including them above

# I was really confused on this part because everything started to change every time I ran my code to double check that it was working. But  I now understand that the point of this is to create some variation based on random data generated by R.
#set.seed then allows me to run the same randomly generated data without creating a new set every time
```
